original_question: Suppose a positive series has remainder terms r_n = sum_{i>n} x_i satisfying r_n > x_n for every n. Must there exist a subsequence (x_{n_k}) whose achievement set E(x_{n_k}) is a Cantorval?
target_in_paper: Section 1, Problem 5: the open problem about thinning out a slowly convergent series to obtain a Cantorval achievement set.
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the core content of the paper's target problem: it uses the original remainder condition r_n > x_n for every n, asks for the existence of a subsequence, and asks whether the achievement set of that subsequence must be a Cantorval. This is exactly the mathematical direction of Section 1, Problem 5.
missing_details: The paper is working in the one-dimensional real setting: a convergent series of positive real numbers, not an arbitrary signed or vector-valued series.

To make the question stand alone, the sequence should be specified as a nonincreasing sequence of positive reals with sum \sum_{n=1}^\infty x_n < \infty, which is the standard Kakeya/achievement-set framework used in the surrounding discussion.
The remainder terms should be defined explicitly as r_n := \sum_{m>n} x_m for the original sequence.
The subsequence should be specified as an infinite subsequence (x_{n_k}) with n_1 < n_2 < \cdots.
The achievement set should be defined explicitly: E(x_{n_k}) := {\sum_{k=1}^\infty \varepsilon_k x_{n_k} : \varepsilon_k \in \{0,1\}}.
The term 'Cantorval' should be made explicit, e.g. as a compact subset of \mathbb{R} homeomorphic to the Guthrie-Nymann model Cantorval.
It should be clear that the problem concerns the topological type of the achievement set of the subseries determined by the subsequence, not the original series.
The nearby context identifies this as a 'thinning out slowly convergent series' problem; that motivation is absent from the draft.
Problem 6 in the paper is only a geometric-sequence restriction of this question, not an equivalent reformulation, so it should not replace Problem 5.
justification: The draft is aiming at Section 1, Problem 5, not at a broader neighboring conjecture. The surrounding paragraph introduces the problem as one about 'thinning out slowly convergent series': every such sequence has a fast convergent subsequence whose achievement set is a Cantor set, but known results also show that under an additional restriction one cannot obtain a Cantorval by thinning out; this motivates the precise open question in Problem 5. The immediately following Problem 6 is only the special case for geometric sequences, so it should not be used as a replacement or an 'equivalent' reformulation. The paper does not present your target as Conjecture 1.1/Proposition 1.2/Theorem 1.3; in this paper it appears explicitly as Problem 5 in Section 1.
